items.title: People judge larger bodies as more forgiving, study suggests
items.summary:
A recent study found that people in China tend to view individuals with larger bodies as more forgiving than those with thinner bodies. This perception seems to stem from a tendency to judge heavier individuals as warmer and more approachable. The research was published in the British Journal of Psychology .

When humans form first impressions, they rely heavily on visual cues to guess a stranger’s moral character. Psychologists often use a framework called the Stereotype Content Model to understand these rapid judgments. This model suggests that people evaluate strangers along two main dimensions: warmth, which involves kindness and trustworthiness, and competence, which involves intelligence and confidence.

Past studies have shown that observers frequently stereotype heavier individuals as warmer but less competent than thinner individuals. Observers also rely on mental shortcuts to assume that if someone possesses one trait, they naturally possess related characteristics. Because the concept of forgivingness overlaps with warmth, an observer might automatically assume a warm-seeming person is also quick to pardon an offense.

Past research has mostly examined what makes a person actually forgiving, linking the trait to personality factors like agreeableness. Less is understood about how observers decide if someone else is forgiving just by looking at them. In Chinese culture, linguistic idioms directly connect a larger physical size to an accommodating nature. One phrase translates to having a broad mind and a fat body, while another uses a large belly as a metaphor…
items.t: People judge larger bodies as more forgiving, study suggests

items.title: Even when calories and nutrients match, ultraprocessed foods trigger a larger insulin surge
items.summary:
Eating an ultraprocessed meal triggers a substantially higher surge in blood insulin, slightly higher post-meal calorie burning, and a slower shift toward burning carbohydrates compared to a non-ultraprocessed meal with nearly identical nutrients, according to a clinical trial published in Nature Metabolism .

These post-meal metabolic shifts also tracked with how reward-processing areas of the brain reacted to photographs of food, even though volunteers reported liking both types of food equally and bid similar amounts of money for them. Together, the findings indicate that industrial food processing alters how the body and brain respond to a meal through pathways that go beyond calories, fat, sugar, or fiber alone.

From nutrient counts to gut-to-brain reward signals 
 Under the Nova classification system, which groups foods by the extent and purpose of industrial processing, ultraprocessed foods are factory-manufactured formulations created through multiple physical and chemical transformations. Common manufacturing steps include breaking whole crops down into isolated starches, oils, and proteins, heating ingredients under high pressure through extrusion, and adding flavorings, emulsifiers, or colorings rarely used in home kitchens.

Products in this category account for 55 percent of the calories consumed in the United States, according to federal dietary survey data. Large population studies link heavy intake to obesity, metabolic disease, and cancer, though skeptics argue those risks simply reflect excess calories, fat, and sugar rather than processing itself.…
items.t: Even when calories and nutrients match, ultraprocessed foods trigger a larger insulin surge

items.title: Evolutionary hypothesis linking facial symmetry to women’s mating behavior fails to hold up in new study
items.summary:
Women with more symmetrical faces are no more open to casual sex or more sexually active than women with less symmetrical faces once their living environment and relationship status are taken into account, according to a new study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior . Initial comparisons among Polish women hinted at a slight connection between facial symmetry and certain sexual attitudes and behaviors, but that pattern disappeared after researchers accounted for whether participants lived in cities or rural villages. The findings suggest that social and environmental surroundings play a much larger role in shaping women’s sexual lives than subtle variations in facial structure.

No human face is an exact mirror image from left to right. Biologists refer to small, random differences between the left and right sides of the face or body as fluctuating asymmetry, a trait that takes shape mainly before birth and during childhood growth. Because illness, poor nutrition, maternal stress, or difficult living conditions can disrupt balanced two-sided growth, evolutionary researchers have proposed that greater symmetry may act as an outward sign of developmental resilience and physical health, although recent reviews indicate that links between facial symmetry and actual medical health are weak and inconsistent.

That evolutionary framework prompted psychologists to test whether physical symmetry shapes human mating behavior, beginning with an influential 1994 study that found people with more symmetrical bodies reported having more lifetime sexual partners. Later…
items.t: Evolutionary hypothesis linking facial symmetry to women’s mating behavior fails to hold up in new study

items.title: People with ADHD have higher odds of a wide range of gut symptoms, study finds
items.summary:
A meta-analysis of 23 studies found that people with ADHD had 48% higher odds of experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms than people without ADHD. The odds were also elevated for specific symptoms, including irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, and encopresis, the repeated involuntary passing of stool. The paper was published in the Journal of Attention Disorders .

Neurodivergence refers to differences in brain functioning and behavior from what is considered typical. It encompasses conditions such as dyslexia, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ADHD is estimated to affect about 5% of children and 3% to 4% of adults.

Although both genetic and environmental factors appear to contribute to these conditions, their exact causes remain incompletely understood. Recent research has increasingly focused on the gut-brain axis, the communication system connecting the gastrointestinal tract and the brain. Studies have found that people with ASD, OCD, and ADHD tend to have somewhat different compositions of gut microorganisms than people without these conditions.

Researchers have proposed that imbalances in gut microorganisms may activate the gut’s immune system and produce low-grade inflammation, contributing to gastrointestinal problems. Consistent with this possibility, people with ASD are more likely to experience gastrointestinal symptoms such as constipation, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, and people with OCD show high rates of bowel disorders.

Study author Sarah Blake of the University…
items.t: People with ADHD have higher odds of a wide range of gut symptoms, study finds

items.title: Psychologists find a hidden asymmetry in how people judge potential partners
items.summary:
When people think about what they want in a romantic partner, they tend to name more positive qualities than negative ones, yet they agree far less on which flaws to avoid. New research published in European Journal of Social Psychology suggests that desirable partner traits cluster tightly around a shared ideal, whereas undesirable traits span a much wider range of meanings. Because people vary so much in the flaws they reject, negative traits turned out to be much more informative than positive ones for predicting hypothetical online dating decisions.

Online dating platforms require users to form quick impressions of strangers from brief text descriptions and a handful of photos. Most psychological research on partner preferences has focused on the specific meaning, or content, of the personality traits people seek, identifying widely desired qualities such as warmth, kindness, intelligence, and trustworthiness. Rather than looking only at what individual traits mean, psychologists can also examine their broader structural patterns, specifically how frequently positive and negative traits come to mind and how closely traits of the same type resemble one another.

Work in social cognition indicates that good and bad traits are not simple mirror images of each other. For instance, a 2012 study of person descriptions found that adults naturally used a much wider variety of words when describing people they disliked than when describing people they liked. Building on similar patterns across language and memory, researchers introduced the Evaluative Information Ecology model…
items.t: Psychologists find a hidden asymmetry in how people judge potential partners

items.title: Criticism from Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan cut Trump’s sway over Republicans in half in experiment on the Epstein files
items.summary:
Republican voters tend to follow Donald Trump’s lead even when he takes an unpopular stance, yet new experimental research published in Public Opinion Quarterly indicates that his influence has limits. Examining the controversy over releasing government records tied to Jeffrey Epstein, the study found that pushback from Democratic lawmakers failed to dent Trump’s sway, whereas counterarguments from conservative media personalities Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan cut his influence on policy attitudes and lowered his approval ratings. The findings suggest that apparent blind loyalty to a dominant political leader may stem less from an unbreakable cult of personality than from a shortage of trusted opposition within the leader’s own ideological camp.

Democratic government rests on political accountability, the idea that citizens monitor what elected officials do and withdraw support when leaders act against public wishes. In practice, public opinion research frequently documents the opposite pattern, known as opinion leadership, in which partisans adjust their own policy preferences to match whatever stance their favored politicians announce. For instance, a 2015 field experiment with U.S. state legislators and their constituents found that when lawmakers sent letters staking out policy positions that conflicted with voters’ earlier views, constituents tended to adopt the legislators’ positions rather than rate those officials more negatively.

No modern political figure has prompted more debate over partisan cue-following than Donald Trump. In a 2018 survey experiment with…
items.t: Criticism from Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan cut Trump’s sway over Republicans in half in experiment on the Epstein files

items.title: Psychiatrists reveal unusual case in which 71-year-old farmer asked to be tied with ropes to calm his severe anxiety
items.summary:
A recent medical case report describes an unusual behavior in an older man who repeatedly asked his relatives to tie him to his bed with ropes during episodes of overwhelming inner restlessness. Published in The Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders , the report suggests that severe anxiety in late life can sometimes manifest through unexpected physical actions rather than classic emotional complaints. Recognizing these atypical signs may help doctors start appropriate treatment and avoid mistaking treatable anxiety for psychotic or neurological illnesses.

Generalized anxiety disorder involves chronic, hard-to-control worry about everyday life, and it can occur alongside panic attacks, which are sudden surges of intense fear and physical tension. While younger adults tend to describe feeling nervous or fearful, older adults frequently express anxiety through somatic symptoms, meaning emotional distress shows up primarily as physical bodily complaints or persistent health worries.

When an elderly patient displays intense agitation and unusual behaviors, clinicians can easily confuse anxiety with other serious conditions. Doctors must consider psychosis, which involves a loss of contact with reality such as delusions or hallucinations, as well as delirium, a sudden state of mental confusion often triggered by physical illness. Unusual late-life behaviors can also resemble neurocognitive disorders like dementia, which cause progressive declines in memory and thinking.

Clinicians also look for akathisia, an agonizing feeling of inner restlessness and an inability to…
items.t: Psychiatrists reveal unusual case in which 71-year-old farmer asked to be tied with ropes to calm his severe anxiety

items.title: Antagonistic and impulsive traits are linked to cyberbullying, trolling, and catfishing on Instagram
items.summary:
A survey of Iranian university students found that those with more pronounced Antagonism and Disinhibition, two maladaptive personality traits, were more likely to report harmful online behaviors such as cyberbullying, trolling, and catfishing. In contrast, students higher in Anankastia, a trait marked by perfectionism and rigid rule-following, were less likely to report several of these behaviors. The paper was published in BMC Psychology .

Social media has become an important part of everyday life. It allows people to communicate, maintain relationships, and connect with communities around the world. However, these platforms can also facilitate harmful behaviors, including cyberbullying, cyberstalking, online fraud, trolling, and various other forms of online aggression. Such behaviors can have serious consequences for victims, including financial losses, emotional distress, anxiety, and depression.

Researchers have increasingly investigated whether personality traits are associated with people’s likelihood of engaging in harmful online behaviors. Previous studies have found that individuals who are less agreeable, less conscientious, and more emotionally unstable tend to report higher levels of various antisocial online behaviors. However, most research has focused on normal personality traits, while relatively little is known about the relationships between harmful online behaviors and maladaptive personality traits, which represent more extreme and potentially dysfunctional patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving.

Study author Mojtaba Elhami Athar of the…

items.title: Prolonged mask exposure changes how we process facial emotions
items.summary:
Humans rely heavily on facial expressions to navigate social interactions, a process that became notably more difficult when face masks became a global norm. Recent research published in Cognition and Emotion reveals that people adapt and improve their ability to read masked emotions over a period of several months. The findings suggest that our visual processing adjusts to occluded faces, and these changes relate to both daily exposure and individual mental health symptoms.

Reading emotions from the faces of others dictates how people respond in social situations. Seeing fear might prompt someone to look for a threat, while a smiling face reinforces positive behaviors. Because human beings rely heavily on the lower half of the face to decode many of these emotional states, facial coverings create a substantial barrier to everyday communication. 

Initial studies during the pandemic revealed that face masks led to lower accuracy and slower reaction times when identifying emotions. It was not well understood whether prolonged exposure to masked faces would eventually lead to improved recognition skills. Past research yielded mixed results, with some data indicating no improvement in adults over time and other data suggesting young children might adapt.

In addition to visual barriers, an individual’s mental state can alter how they perceive emotions in others. Some research indicates that people experiencing depression might be better at recognizing sadness, while those with anxiety might be highly sensitive to fearful faces. Researchers wanted to know how these mood…
items.t: Prolonged mask exposure changes how we process facial emotions

items.title: Mild sleep loss can dull how much people enjoy art and perceive beauty
items.summary:
Getting a couple of hours less sleep than usual for just two nights may subtly dull how much people enjoy artwork and perceive its beauty, according to new experimental research published in Journal of Sleep Research . In a controlled sleep-laboratory study of young adults, mild sleep restriction dampened morning alertness and positive mood while lowering ratings of abstract paintings, though it did not alter judgments based on the perceived race or gender of the artist. The findings suggest that adequate rest does more than prevent fatigue and mistakes, playing a quiet role in how people appreciate everyday aesthetic experiences.

Aesthetics refers to how people perceive and respond emotionally to beauty, art, and design in the world around them. Those responses depend partly on visual features of an object, such as symmetry or color, and partly on what the viewer brings to the moment, including cultural background, personality, and mood. Psychologists studying art appreciation frequently use abstract paintings, which rely on shapes, colors, and textures rather than recognizable everyday scenes, leaving their meaning open to personal interpretation and creating wide variation from one viewer to the next.

Health guidelines generally recommend at least seven hours of sleep per night for adults, and falling short is well known to impair attention, memory, academic performance, and job satisfaction. Losing sleep also alters emotional life, though not always in the way people assume. Rather than uniformly fueling anger or distress, a 2023 meta-analysis of 154 experimental…
items.t: Mild sleep loss can dull how much people enjoy art and perceive beauty

items.title: The earlier kids join social media, the lower their test scores tend to be, study finds
items.summary:
A study of high school students in Lombardy, a region in northern Italy, found that students who created a personal social media account in 6th, 7th, or 8th grade tended to score lower on standardized tests of Italian and mathematics than peers who waited until 9th grade or later. The earlier students opened an account, the larger the gap tended to be. The paper was published in Nature Human Behaviour .

The age at which children should be allowed to start using smartphones and social media has become a subject of intense debate among scientists, educators, and parents. Children are increasingly acquiring their first smartphones at around 10 or 11 years of age, often creating social media accounts before reaching the minimum age required by platforms or national regulations. This trend has raised concerns because increasing digital media use among young people has coincided with declining indicators of mental health and academic performance in many countries.

Research suggests that intensive social media use is associated with poorer sleep, reduced concentration, fewer face-to-face interactions, and lower life satisfaction. However, scientists disagree about whether social media use directly causes these problems, as findings have been inconsistent and many studies cannot establish cause-and-effect relationships.

Studies examining academic performance have generally found small negative associations between social media use and learning outcomes, although much of this research has focused on university students. Another important limitation is that researchers have…

items.title: Your brain may start reacting to an emoji’s expression before your eyes even reach it
items.summary:
When people read a text message containing a smiling face emoji, their brains may begin registering its emotional tone before their eyes even look directly at it, according to new eye-tracking research published in Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology . The experiment indicates that an upcoming positive face emoji is associated with readers pausing slightly longer on the preceding word than a neutral face emoji is, while also finishing the overall sentence slightly faster. Together, the findings provide evidence that readers take in emotional symbols alongside neighboring words in parallel rather than processing each item strictly one at a time.

Emojis are small pictorial symbols depicting faces, gestures, objects, and animals that people insert into digital messages to convey emotion and tone, serving a role similar to facial expressions in spoken conversation. People tend to be remarkably quick at reading these tiny faces: an earlier emotion-recognition experiment found that participants identified emotions 73 milliseconds faster and more accurately from emojis than from photographs of real human faces, with happy expressions recognized fastest of all.

Matching symbols can also shape how an entire message lands, as an earlier study of social media posts indicated that tweets paired with an emotionally fitting emoji were judged easier to understand and more believable than tweets with mismatched emojis or none at all.

Beyond overall message impressions, psychologists use high-speed eye-tracking cameras to examine how emojis alter the split-second mechanics of…
items.t: Your brain may start reacting to an emoji’s expression before your eyes even reach it

items.title: Men and women mostly agree on gender roles, except for one surprising area
items.summary:
A new psychological measurement tool allows scientists to assess what people believe men and women should do at work and at home without forcing those expectations into an either-or tradeoff. Developed and validated in a study published in Sex Roles , the new scales measure beliefs about caregiving and career roles separately for each gender on an identical rating scale. Initial testing indicates that the tool performs consistently across male and female respondents and predicts attitudes such as feminist identity and willingness to confront everyday sexism better than an established alternative.

Prescriptive gender role beliefs are ideas about how men and women ought to behave and which responsibilities should fall to each gender in daily life. In the United States, gender continues to shape how people divide their time, even though 91% of Americans report that gender equality is very important. Women make up nearly half of the workforce, yet national time-use data show they spend an average of 40 minutes more per day than men on household chores like cooking and cleaning, while working men in heterosexual couples enjoy two more hours of leisure time each week, a gap that widens to four and a half hours among parents of young children.

Measuring how people think about these roles has proven surprisingly difficult. A 1990 handbook cataloged 235 measures related to gender roles, yet many existing questionnaires rely on dated phrasing, such as asking whether it is ridiculous for a woman to run a locomotive or for a man to darn socks, which nearly everyone now rejects.…
items.t: Men and women mostly agree on gender roles, except for one surprising area

items.title: Scientists uncover how early life stress rewires the brain
items.summary:
Early life stress can alter how DNA is packaged in the brain, making individuals more vulnerable to adversity later in life. By mimicking these molecular changes in young mice, researchers were able to artificially program a lifelong sensitivity to stressful events. The findings were published in * The Journal of Neuroscience *.

Early life experiences shape the developing brain through a process known as epigenetics. Epigenetic mechanisms involve chemical tags that attach to DNA or its packaging proteins, called histones. These tags do not change the underlying genetic code. Instead, they dictate whether specific genes are accessible and active at any given time.

DNA does not float freely in a cell; it is tightly spooled around histone proteins to form a complex known as chromatin. When chromatin is tightly packed, genes are hidden and turned off. When it is loosely packed, the genes become accessible to the cellular machinery that reads them. 

The nucleus accumbens is a region deep in the brain that helps process rewards, emotions, and responses to stressful events. In this area, a specific epigenetic tag known as H3K4me1 acts as a molecular bookmark. This bookmark keeps certain sections of the chromatin slightly open. 

By keeping the chromatin open, the tag primes those genetic regions to be activated quickly in response to future environmental stimuli. Researchers Catherine Jensen Peña of Princeton University and Meaghan C. Creed of Washington University in St. Louis led a team to investigate this mechanism. Along with lead authors Rebekah L. Rashford and Lisa Z.…
items.t: Scientists uncover how early life stress rewires the brain

items.title: New psychology research sheds light on why certain pop song hooks stick in your head
items.summary:
Listeners judge musical hooks in unfamiliar pop songs as more attention-grabbing and memorable when they hear the songs multiple times, while an auditory verbal distraction makes those hooks feel less catchy, according to new research published in Psychology of Music . Across two laboratory experiments, chorus sections consistently stood out over other parts of a song even when listeners were distracted, suggesting that catchy pop phrases rely on both songwriting structure and human memory and attention.

In popular music, a hook is a distinct melodic, rhythmic, or lyrical phrase that grabs a listener’s attention and sticks easily in memory, such as the repeating nonsense syllables in Kylie Minogue’s “Can’t Get You Out of My Head.” Because modern pop recordings layer vocals, drums, bass, and harmonies all at once, the brain cannot process every detail equally and instead filters for standout moments. Researchers think these phrases lodge in verbal working memory, the short-term mental workspace often described as an “inner voice” that lets people silently rehearse words and melodies.

Earlier music psychology research began tracing how repetition and attention shape this process, particularly in relation to earworms, the everyday experience of a musical snippet looping involuntarily in the mind. For instance, a 2015 experiment co-authored by one of the new study’s researchers found that playing unfamiliar songs repeatedly made those tunes more likely to resurface spontaneously later on. Meanwhile, a 2021 pair of laboratory experiments indicated that catchy songs occupy…
items.t: New psychology research sheds light on why certain pop song hooks stick in your head

items.title: What two decades of psychology and neuroscience research say about playing Grand Theft Auto
items.summary:
Few entertainment franchises have attracted as much cultural attention and public anxiety as Grand Theft Auto . With the November 2026 launch of Grand Theft Auto VI ending a 13-year wait, the video game series is once again drawing massive audiences and renewed scrutiny.

The franchise began in 1997 as a top-down, two-dimensional crime game, and its 2001 entry, Grand Theft Auto III , moved the action into a fully three-dimensional city that players could roam freely. Across the series, players steal cars, complete criminal missions, and attack bystanders, while later installments added mundane pastimes like bowling and getting haircuts.

When Grand Theft Auto V launched in 2013, it grossed $1 billion faster than any entertainment product in history. That cultural reach has long invited questions from lawmakers, journalists, and parents about whether stepping into the shoes of a virtual criminal changes how people think, feel, and behave once they put down the controller.

Over the past two decades, psychologists, neuroscientists, and criminologists have used the franchise to put that question to the test. They have measured players’ anger and blood pressure, scanned their brains for signs of dulled empathy, tracked teenagers for years, and compared game release dates against national crime records.

The evidence has rarely pointed in a single direction. Some effects show up within minutes of play and others fail to appear after months, and a few studies have set off public disputes among the researchers themselves.

items.t: What two decades of psychology and neuroscience research say about playing Grand Theft Auto

items.title: Acceptance and commitment therapy linked to neural shifts in the depressed brain
items.summary:
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy reduces depression symptoms and is associated with changes in brain activity in areas responsible for emotional regulation. Brain scans of adults with major depressive disorder showed that this specific therapeutic approach alters neural connectivity related to obsessive, negative thinking. The small study was published in Brain Imaging and Behavior .

Major depressive disorder is a widespread psychiatric condition that causes persistent sadness and a lack of interest in life. While antidepressant medications and traditional talk therapies help many people, a large portion of patients do not experience full recovery. Because of this, mental health professionals continue to explore alternative therapeutic methods.

One such method is Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. Unlike traditional cognitive behavioral therapy, which attempts to change the content of a person’s negative thoughts, this alternative encourages people to change their relationship with those thoughts. The goal is to build psychological flexibility so that patients can live a meaningful life even when experiencing internal distress.

A primary concept in this therapy is cognitive fusion. This happens when individuals treat their internal verbal thoughts as absolute truths or literal reality, rather than just passing mental events. For instance, a person might have the thought “I am a burden” and treat it as a factual reality, leading to psychological distress and avoidance behaviors.

items.t: Acceptance and commitment therapy linked to neural shifts in the depressed brain

items.title: Neuroimaging study links heightened sensitivity to peer rejection with harsher parenting after childhood abuse
items.summary:
More severe childhood abuse is linked to harsher discipline of teenagers among mothers whose brains react more strongly to social rejection than to social approval, according to a study published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience .

Among mothers without this heightened brain reactivity to negative social feedback, abuse severity was not associated with harsher parenting. The findings suggest that how the adult brain processes interpersonal slights and acceptance may help identify which families face greater risk of carrying mistreatment across generations.

Why childhood abuse does not always lead to harsh parenting 
 Childhood maltreatment includes abuse, involving physical, emotional, or sexual acts that harm or threaten a child, and neglect, the failure to provide expected care and stimulation. Mistreated children are two to three times more likely to mistreat their own children as parents, often through harsh discipline such as yelling, verbal hostility, physical punishment, or punishing without explanation. Evidence from a 2019 meta-analysis of 142 studies indicates that abuse persists across generations more consistently than neglect.

Because abuse involves interpersonal threat, how people process social feedback, meaning signals of approval, criticism, or rejection, may shape intergenerational risk. Adults who survived childhood abuse tend to display a negativity bias, such as reading neutral faces as angry or viewing ambiguous child behavior as defiant. Consistent with this, a 2011 longitudinal study of 499 mothers and their infants found that…
items.t: Neuroimaging study links heightened sensitivity to peer rejection with harsher parenting after childhood abuse

items.title: Reanalysis of 1950s LSD experiments challenges the idea that psychedelics make art more creative
items.summary:
Professional artists who painted under the influence of LSD produced markedly more abstract works than they did before taking the drug, according to a new reanalysis of archived mid-century artworks published in Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts . At the same time, blind evaluations by art experts detected no meaningful boost in the paintings’ overall creativity or aesthetic appeal, and no reliable drop in technical skill. The findings indicate that while psychedelic experiences can shift an artist’s visual style toward abstraction, they do not necessarily make the finished work more creative.

Lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly known as LSD, is a potent hallucinogenic substance that alters visual perception, emotion, and thought primarily by stimulating specific serotonin receptors in the brain. Alongside renewed clinical interest in psychedelic substances over the past two decades, anecdotal accounts from technology workplaces and visual arts communities have popularized the claim that taking LSD in either tiny microdoses or full hallucinogenic amounts can unlock artistic breakthroughs. Yet subjective impressions during a drug experience can be misleading, making it difficult to tell whether a substance genuinely improves creative work or merely makes ideas feel deeper in the moment.

In psychological science, creativity is typically defined as the ability to produce something that is both original and fitting or effective for its context. Reaching that balance requires two complementary modes of thinking: divergent thinking, which involves loosening…
items.t: Reanalysis of 1950s LSD experiments challenges the idea that psychedelics make art more creative

items.title: Common classroom accommodations for ADHD fail to improve student behavior or schoolwork in clinical trial
items.summary:
A clinical trial published in JAMA Pediatrics provides evidence that four widely used classroom accommodations for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) do not improve student behavior or academic performance. In contrast, structured behavioral classroom supports and a moderate dose of stimulant medication both substantially reduced classroom rule-breaking, while medication also increased assignment completion and quiz scores.

The findings suggest that schools seeking to help students with ADHD succeed may achieve better results from active behavioral strategies than from standard classroom accommodations.

Why classroom accommodations for ADHD needed a test 
 ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by ongoing difficulties sustaining attention, curbing impulsive actions, and regulating physical restlessness. In elementary school classrooms, those traits frequently surface as trouble staying seated, following classroom rules, completing independent worksheets, and keeping up with group lessons.

In the United States, roughly half of students diagnosed with ADHD receive formal educational services through individualized education programs under federal special education law or Section 504 plans under disability civil rights law. These plans routinely center on academic accommodations, which are adjustments to classroom surroundings, work schedules, or testing conditions meant to help students complete the same assignments as their classmates. Common examples include extra time on assignments and quizzes, frequent short breaks,…
items.t: Common classroom accommodations for ADHD fail to improve student behavior or schoolwork in clinical trial

items.title: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth
items.summary:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth. 

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020 . What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017 .

As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens , a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to…
items.t: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

items.title: I’m engaged but I can’t stop thinking about an old friend. Should I tell him how I feel? | Leading questions
items.summary:
Telling him would risk a lot of harm, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. If you’re going to take that gamble, you’d better be sure why you’re doing it

  • Read more Leading questions

My partner and I are engaged after a whirlwind romance, and I was over the moon when he proposed. He is a wonderful, kind and generous man, and will be an amazing husband. However, I’ve since found out that a friend I’ve known for years has always carried a torch for me, and this knowledge has made me see him in a different light. I can’t stop thinking about him, and it’s making me question if I should marry my fiance. My friend has no idea I feel this way, and has recently got engaged, so nothing has obviously changed, apart from my feelings.

Do I continue with planning my wedding and push these new feelings down, or do I tell my friend how I feel in case he still feels the same? This indecision is torturing me.

items.title: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents
items.summary:
It was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the new baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge. 

Emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s important to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own.

items.t: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents

items.title: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?
items.summary:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure , an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

items.t: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?
